q: How does coding for ML differ from traditional software engineering?
short: Traditional: developers write explicit rules, logic in code, goal is correct functionality, bugs fixed in code, rules inspectable. ML: systems learn rules from data, logic in parameters, goal is generalisation, fixes via data/features/training, harder to interpret.
detail: Both still need good code around the model.
mistakes: Testing only the code, not the data.

q: What are the features of good code?
short: Simplicity, modularity, readability, performance and robustness.
follow: Which matters most in research code?

q: What is DRY and why does it matter in ML?
short: Don't repeat yourself: each piece of logic should exist once. In ML, duplicated preprocessing or feature code drifts between copies and between training and serving, causing silent errors and skew.
detail: Hotspots: preprocessing, features, training loops, deployment.

q: What does pylint do?
short: Static analysis: reports errors, style violations (PEP 8), naming issues, unused imports/variables, duplicated or complex code and missing docstrings, with a score out of 10.

q: time vs timeit?
short: time measures one elapsed run (low accuracy, includes warm-up, good for whole workflows); timeit repeats many runs and reports mean ± sd (higher accuracy, good for comparing implementations).

q: What does a profiler tell you?
short: Where a program spends time (or memory), by function (cProfile) or by line (line_profiler), so you optimise the real bottleneck.

q: List ways to make Python code faster.
short: Better algorithm; better data structure; built-ins and vectorised libraries (NumPy, pandas); asynchronous I/O; parallel or distributed computing.
detail: Order of impact usually algorithm first.
mistakes: Parallelising an O(n²) algorithm instead of fixing it.

q: What makes code robust?
short: Reproducible results, runs end-to-end, handles errors gracefully with useful messages, handles unexpected inputs, logs behaviour, and is tested.
example: Clear error when a column is missing.

q: Why prefer descriptive names over X, y, m?
short: They document intent, reduce mistakes and satisfy style guides; pylint flags non-snake_case names (C0103).
detail: Readability is a feature of good code.

q: tottime vs cumtime in cProfile?
short: tottime is time spent inside the function itself; cumtime includes all functions it calls. High cumtime but low tottime means the cost is in callees.
detail: Sort by cumulative to find the top-level culprit.

q: Benchmark two implementations fairly.
short: Use timeit.repeat with enough repeats and number, same inputs, warm-up excluded, report mean ± sd (or min), isolate the machine, and check results are identical.
follow: Why might min be better than mean?

q: A training script got 3x slower after a refactor. How do you investigate?
short: Reproduce with fixed data, time both versions with timeit, profile both with cProfile and compare cumtime, drill into the hotspot with line_profiler, check data types (object vs float), copies and I/O.

q: How do you refactor a notebook into good code?
short: Extract repeated cells into functions with clear inputs/outputs, move them into modules, add docstrings and type hints, lint and format, add tests, keep the notebook as a thin driver.

q: Your timing sd is 30% of the mean. What does it mean and what do you do?
short: Measurements are noisy: background load, CPU frequency scaling, caching, GC. Increase repeats, use min or median, pin CPU, close other processes, warm up, and benchmark on a dedicated machine.
mistakes: Concluding a 5% speed-up from noisy data.

q: How do you find a memory leak in a Python ML service?
short: Track memory over requests; use memray or tracemalloc snapshots to compare allocations over time and find growing call sites; check caches without bounds, global lists, retained tensors/graphs and unclosed resources.
detail: Memory profilers show which line allocates.
example: Appending every request to a global list.

q: Why can Python loops be 100x slower than NumPy?
short: Each loop iteration runs interpreted bytecode with dynamic type checks and boxed objects; NumPy runs a compiled C loop over contiguous typed memory, often with SIMD.

q: How do you enforce code quality across a data-science team?
short: Shared style guide, formatter and linter in pre-commit hooks and CI, type checking, code review, templates for project structure, and tests required for shared modules.

q: What is the difference between a linter and a formatter?
short: A formatter (black) rewrites code layout deterministically; a linter (pylint, ruff, flake8) analyses code for errors, smells and style violations without necessarily changing it.
example: black for layout, pylint for unused imports.
follow: What does a type checker add?

q: Explain Amdahl's law and its relevance to optimisation.
short: Speed-up = 1 / ((1−p) + p/s), where p is the fraction of time improved and s its speed-up. Optimising a small fraction yields little; target the dominant bottleneck found by profiling.
detail: fit at 63% bounds total gain to ~2.7x.
example: Infinite speed-up of load_iris (19.5%) gives at most 1.24x.

q: Profiling shows 60% of inference latency in feature preprocessing. Options?
short: Vectorise or precompute features, cache static lookups, move to a feature store, compile with Numba/Cython, reduce data copies, batch requests, and ensure training uses the same optimised code.

q: What are the limitations of cProfile?
short: Function-level only, adds overhead (especially for many small calls), doesn't see inside C extensions by line, not ideal for multithreaded/async code, and measures CPU time of Python calls, not I/O waits clearly. Use sampling profilers (py-spy, scalene) for production.
detail: Pick the tool for the question.
mistakes: Profiling in production with heavy overhead.

q: Design a performance-regression check for an ML library.
short: Benchmark suite with fixed data sizes (pytest-benchmark/asv), run on dedicated CI hardware, store history, compare against baseline with tolerance based on observed variance, and alert on significant regressions.
example: Fail CI if fit is >10% slower.

q: How do you balance research speed with code quality?
short: Use lightweight standards early (formatter, linter, seeds, small functions), invest more as code becomes shared or moves toward production; refactor before handover, not after an incident.
detail: Research vs production code in M10.

q: How do you make ML code reproducible?
short: Fix random seeds, pin library versions, version data and code, record configs and environment, avoid nondeterministic GPU ops where needed, and log run metadata.
